title: The Dragon Who Loved Snowflakes
markdown:
Witch Mabli’s boots crunched on the packed snow. Glacialift’s air was so crisp it felt like biting an icicle. Beside her, Wisp, a snow hare the colour of a winter storm, hopped along. His ears twitched like nervous antennae. His nose was a constant sniff-and-explore device. They were here to judge the Festival of Frosty Feats. Mabli, practical as ever, had agreed for the prize money. It would finally fix her leaky cauldron.

Glacialift was a dizzying delightful marvel. Frozen roads snaked up the mountain like icy serpents. High in the thin air, markets shimmered under ice arches. Wool banners snapped like tiny flags, shouting about frozen feats. The air smelled of roasting nuts and something acrid, like burnt sugar or a dragon’s sneeze. “Quite the spectacle, isn’t it, Wisp?” Mabli murmured. Ice sculptors carved frost-breathing beasts. Fire dancers swirled controlled flames. A man with a red nose juggled frozen fish that thumped with each catch.

Then they saw him: a creature of immense scale and shimmering obsidian. Ignis, a dragon. He was not roaring or breathing fire. He was carefully, painstakingly, building an ice sculpture of a tiny delicate snowflake. His movements were slow, deliberate, almost fragile. It was odd. Like a thundercloud trying to knit.

Mabli, who noticed the smallest wobble in a broomstick, tilted her head. “Interesting medium for a dragon, wouldn’t you agree, Wisp?” she said dryly. Wisp was busy trying to reassemble a discarded gingerbread man with enthusiastic licks. “And such intricate work. One might worry about accidental fumigations, given the general volcanic nature of your species.”

Ignis’s colossal head snapped up. His voice was a low rumble that vibrated in Mabli’s bones. “Accidental fumigations? Madam Witch, my control is impeccable. This snowflake,” he declared, puffing out his chest and sending icicles raining down, “represents the transient beauty of winter. A delicate art, not for the heavy-handed or the unobservant.” His wings gave a nervous flutter.

Mabli blinked. “Oh, I didn’t doubt your control, Ignis. Not at all. More that a creature of your stature, with your magnificent fire-breathing, might melt it with a casual sigh. It’s just very small.”

Wisp nudged her. The dragon’s scales had dimmed. He turned away, tail sweeping snow into a miniature avalanche. “Small?” His voice was a wounded whisper. “You find my dedication to detail small?”

“He looks sad, Mabli,” Wisp said. “Like when I lost my favourite dandelion puff. His sparkle is gone.”

Mabli sighed. She was not a diplomat for sensitive dragons, and she almost refused the whole messy business of feelings in favour of cauldrons and scores. Wisp, mentor of the blunt, kept hopping until she had to follow. “It’s not small in skill, Ignis,” she tried, still too blunt. “It’s small in scale. Most dragons sculpt mountains. Not frost flowers. It’s impressive, of course, but unexpected.” The words hung. The festival continued. Ignis performed with less grandeur, pride bruised like a cracked ice crystal.

They had crossed into it now: not a judging booth but a creature’s weather. The final event was the Flight of Fancy. Ignis was supposed to perform an aerial ballet. His heart was not in it. He soared, wings beating powerfully, but his movements were jerky. He nearly collided with a towering icicle spire shaped like a stoic mountain troll. Chunks of ice rained down near the spectators. The crowd gasped.

Wisp squeaked on Mabli’s shoulder, clutching her cloak. “He’s still thinking about the snowflake. He’s not flying with his chest. He’s flying with his hurt feelings.”

Mabli saw the unintentional chaos. The prize money receded. This was about a magnificent creature in distress. She scrambled down from her judging seat. Wisp guided her through the crowd. The ordeal arrived as three things at once: the cold slap of ice-dust on her cheeks, the iron taste of worry, the rumble in her bones as he descended. “Ignis,” she called. “If you are going to be mysterious, you could at least be punctual with your near-disasters.”

The dragon faltered. His grand loop turned into a wobbly circle. Slowly, with a rumble that shook snow from nearby stalls, he landed. He looked magnificent, but forlorn. Golden eyes held deep sadness.

“I apologise,” Mabli began, awkward; she was not used to apologising to dragons. “My observation about the snowflake was blunt. Perhaps too blunt for an artist of your calibre. I meant it was impressive because it was so detailed, so intricate, so unlike the grand gestures one often sees from creatures of your magnitude. It was a testament to your incredible control.” She gestured to Wisp, who hopped forward. “He noticed. He saw your feelings were hurt. I was so focused on the why, the practicalities, I forgot to appreciate the how. The sheer beauty of your delicate craft.”

Wisp nudged Ignis’s colossal sapphire-blue toe. “It was the prettiest snowflake,” he squeaked. “And your sky-dancing was almost as good as a good chase after a runaway cheese roll, which is very, very good.”

Ignis looked from Mabli to Wisp. Surprise. Wonder. He had not expected an apology from a witch who looked as if she’d rather be brewing potions, nor from an even smaller hare. The unexpectedness of it melted something in him, a frozen knot of pride and misunderstanding.

A low rumbling chuckle echoed through Glacialift, free of hurt, tinged with amusement. “You see,” Ignis said, majestic again but warm, “even dragons have their artistic sensitivities. And their rather keen judges, it seems.” He nudged Mabli gently with his snout. The crowd had gathered.

The reward was friendship. The hidden cost revealed itself on the road back through the stalls: the official judges, a stern-faced gnome and a perpetually flustered yeti, were in an uproar. Ice sculptures good. Fire dancers dazzling. But the real story was the dragon who learned to fly with his heart, and the witch who learned to speak to it. Mabli and Ignis were declared joint honorary judges for life. The prize money would still fix a cauldron. The cost was that she would have to come back, year after year, and be careful with other people’s snowflakes.

Mabli’s boots crunched on the packed snow again, same festival path, different errand. She smiled. She had gained a very unusual, very dignified, and surprisingly sensitive friend. A friend who, she suspected, might occasionally need help with his delicate artistic endeavours, and whose ice-flower still stood, unmelted, under the arches.
characters: Mabli (a practical festival-judging witch), Wisp (a snow hare the colour of a winter storm), Ignis (a dragon trying to seem dignified)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
author: StoryGen Community
